stories.title: Belitung: A beach escape closer to Singapore than Bali
stories.summary: Half the flying time to Bali, and at times for less than half the price. But Belitung does not offer half the experience. Jumping into the warm, turquoise waters off Belitung makes that point quickly. It is slightly hard to believe that Singapore is less than 90 minutes away, and Jakarta about an hour, especially considering the kind of seawater found around both cities. For those living in or passing through Singapore, the island of Belitung off the eastern coast of Sumatra has now become much easier to reach. Scoot began twice-weekly direct flights in May 2026, restoring a connection that had been absent since 2019 due to the pandemic and reopening Belitung to international flights. Make no mistake, Belitung is no Bali. It is smaller, quieter and far less developed for tourism. There are no endless rows of beach clubs and international restaurants, or traffic jams caused by tourists on motorcycles. But after a few days here, it becomes clear why these aspects appeal to certain visitors. Several Singaporeans. I met had come precisely because they wanted somewhere quieter, less crowded and a little less polished.

stories.title: Thai patience wears thin as backlash against ‘bad’ tourists grows
stories.summary: A Phuket protest on Aug 28 highlighted growing local frustration over alleged misbehaviour by foreign visitors. Thailand has introduced tougher rules allowing foreigners who disrupt public order or break the law to be deported and potentially barred from returning. Experts warn that legitimate concerns over tourism and foreign businesses should not become hostility towards entire nationalities or groups. Frustrated by what they see as a spate of incidents involving disrespectful behaviour by foreign visitors, Phuket residents gathered at Patong beach on Aug 28 to call for greater respect for Thai laws and culture. The “Save Phuket” event, attended by an estimated 200 people, took place as Thailand introduced tougher measures allowing the authorities to revoke the visas of foreigners who cause public disturbances, remove them from the country and potentially bar them from returning. A visible backlash against foreigners is emerging in Thailand – from a Phuket beach gathering to vigilante groups – as the government steps up efforts to crack down on foreigners who flout the law, raising questions about where legitimate enforcement ends and hostility towards foreigners begins. The Phuket beach event was organised by a group of local residents who say they want to give Thais a platform to air their frustrations, rather than target foreigners as a whole. The Facebook page for the group, which currently has at least 6,900 followers, carries posters in Thai saying “Phuket will not stay silent” and “Respect Thai law”. One of the organisers, 42-year-old Saichon Nuchet, told. The Straits Times the event provides a platform for local Thais to voice their frustrations over encounters with disrespectful foreigners who flout the law. Saichon, a Phuket native, said the group also wants to prevent the island from gaining a negative reputation because of such incidents. “We do not want Phuket to be portrayed negatively in the news because of violence, disrespect towards business operators, violations of the law, refusing to pay for food or services, or certain individuals receiving special privileges.”

stories.title: West Sumatra, where you find buffalo supermodels and a village called ‘Singapore’
stories.summary: The first thing I noticed about West Sumatra were the horns. They point skywards from the traditional communal Minangkabau houses, known as rumah gadang, and are repeated across the layered roofs of Istano Basa Pagaruyung, the reconstructed royal palace. These roofs mimic the horns of an animal that is commonly found here: the buffalo. A few days later, I went looking for one. My guide Habibie, who goes by one name, and I were looking across Sianok Canyon near Bukittinggi, a highland city about a two-hour drive from the capital Padang, when we spotted several buffaloes grazing below. “Should we go down and look for them?” I asked. “Let’s.” We found them behind a gate, chewing grass and entirely uninterested in our photo shoot. “Mokkk! Mokkk!” Habibie called out, drawing out a long, throaty moo. That, he explained, was how buffaloes sounded. One slowly raised its head and stared straight at my camera.

stories.title: No ghosts, just good food: Pontianak shines on the Equator
stories.summary: For many Singaporeans and Malaysians, the word pontianak might conjure up eerie images of a vengeful female spirit that is said to appear under the full moon – thanks in no small part to Malay horror films and urban myths. But when I arrived in the city of Pontianak in West Kalimantan, I found little trace of this ghostly apparition, despite my best efforts. Legend has it that up till the 18th century, the site where Pontianak now stands was a ghost-infested wilderness, unfit for human habitation. Then, in 1771, Syarif Abdurrahman Alkadrie, a prince of Arab and Malay descent, arrived from nearby Mempawah and drove out all the pontianak (or kuntilanak as they are known in Indonesian) by firing cannons, thus establishing the Sultanate of Pontianak. The sultan’s expedition appears to have been a resounding success, because current-day Pontianak residents do not seem to have any fears that the spirits might show up when it gets dark. There are no ghostly walking tours or designated haunted sites, and a proposal to erect a kuntilanak statue in the city centre was abandoned due to lack of interest. “Oh yes, Pontianak does mean kuntilanak in Malay,” Pontianak native Muhajir, 36, told me when I asked. “But I haven’t really heard of any sightings around here. Maybe further out in the jungle.” As night falls over Pontianak, the lights of a lone riverboat glow against the dark waters of the Kapuas, Indonesia’s longest river, where legend has it that female spirits known as pontianak once lurked. Instead, for locals and Malaysian visitors who come from neighbouring Sarawak, Pontianak has two main claims to fame: being the only city in the world located precisely on the Equator and a bustling culinary scene – a result of the city’s unique blend of Malay, Chinese and Dayak cultures. “There’s so much good food in Pontianak.
